title: The Demand Spike

company.name: Gulf Beverages Co.
company.overview: Gulf Beverages Co. is a fast-growing regional beverage manufacturer serving major retailers and distributors across the Gulf. The company has grown quickly, but its supply chain is under increasing pressure as demand becomes more volatile across markets and product lines.

facts.label: Product Lines
facts.value: Bottled juices, flavoured water, ready-to-drink teas

facts.label: Current Priority
facts.value: Maintain service levels while demand grows across key retail accounts

situation: Demand is up roughly 40% year on year. Service levels are falling, and retailers are threatening to delist two product lines within six weeks. The business is treating this as a demand spike it failed to forecast. Your task is not to solve it yet. It is to figure out what problem is actually worth solving.

stakeholders.name: Rohini Agarwal
stakeholders.blurb: Regional demand planning and forecast coordination
stakeholders.sideNote: Rohini sees demand through forecasts and weekly planning updates. She does not sit in the plant, and she is not the person who places supplier orders.

questions.text: Can you walk us through what changed in the forecast over the last few weeks?
questions.answer: The headline number is a 40% increase, but that hides a lot. The spike is not evenly spread across the business. It's concentrated in two product lines, mainly in UAE and KSA, and mostly through modern trade retailers. Some SKUs are moving much faster than expected, while others are still close to forecast.

questions.text: When did the demand signal start changing, and how was it communicated?
questions.answer: We started seeing unusual movement about three weeks ago, but it wasn't clean enough to trigger a major escalation at first. Some of it looked like normal promotional uplift. Then sales confirmed additional retailer activity quite late, and by the time the forecast was revised, procurement and manufacturing were already working off older assumptions.

questions.text: Where did the planning process break down between sales, procurement, and manufacturing?
questions.answer: I sent the revised number as soon as I had it. Procurement came back and said the orders for that cycle had already gone in against the previous plan. The plant asked me what to put on the line, and I sent them the same uplift percentage, because that is the number I had. Nobody pushed back on me and nothing changed. We talked about it in the Tuesday call, everyone agreed it was tight, and then everyone went back to their own week. I have sent that percentage three times now.

questions.text: What should we understand before deciding whether the solution is more stock, faster production, or different allocation?
questions.answer: I'd want to know whether the most urgent issue is total volume, product mix, or allocation. If the wrong SKUs are in the wrong markets, producing more overall won't solve the retailer problem. We need to identify which products and accounts are at risk, agree on priorities, and then decide whether to shift inventory, adjust production, or renegotiate timelines with retailers.

stakeholders.name: Fatima Al-Harbi
stakeholders.sideNote: Fatima owns supplier lead times and purchase orders. She does not set the production schedule or the forecast.

questions.text: Have any suppliers missed agreed lead times in the last quarter?
questions.answer: Not in a way that explains this. Concentrate orange, sugar, PET resin, and tea extract have all landed inside the windows we contracted. We placed the last cycle of orders against the previous forecast, which is what procurement is supposed to do. I keep getting asked if we were late. We were not late. If manufacturing is waiting on something, it is not because a supplier failed to ship within the agreement.

questions.text: When did you last receive a revised volume request from planning?
questions.answer: A proper revision came through quite late relative to the retailer noise I was hearing from sales. Until then we were covering the old plan plus a modest buffer. I can rush a spot buy, but concentrate and packing materials are not same-week items, and suppliers will not hold open capacity for a number they have not seen. I assumed the issue would be worked downstream once the orders were in.

questions.text: Could you pull extra volume from existing contracts if manufacturing asked this week?
questions.answer: On paper, two suppliers have optional volume, but it is priced as spot and they want an eight-to-ten-week slot, not six. I have not been given a SKU-level breakdown of what would actually be bottled, so I cannot even tell them which drums to expedite. I have been treating this as a factory or allocation problem because my inbound calendar still looks healthy.

questions.text: What can you not see from where you sit?
questions.answer: I do not see which production slots are confirmed, and I do not see which retailers are actually short. Purchase orders look fine on my dashboard. If the plant is refusing short runs or holding a line for a long changeover, that never appears in procurement. I only hear about it when someone asks why the materials are sitting while finished goods are missing.

stakeholders.name: James Okoro
stakeholders.sideNote: James runs the lines and the changeover calendar. He does not own the commercial forecast or retailer conversations.

questions.text: Are the lines actually full, or is something else eating the week?
questions.answer: Utilisation looks high because we batch. The two juice lines that make the fast movers have long flavour changeovers. If I break a run to chase every retailer request, I lose hours, not minutes. We have been protecting economic run length so the cost per case does not blow up. From the floor this looks like a capacity story. I do not get a clean picture of which SKUs are truly off-plan versus which ones just shout the loudest.

questions.text: How do you decide the sequence of SKUs on those constrained lines?
questions.answer: We still sequence from the planning freeze we received, then we try to absorb extras at the end of the week. Planning has been sending an aggregate uplift. An aggregate number does not tell me whether to stay on Mango Nectar or switch to Sparkling Citrus. Switching is expensive. Staying on the wrong SKU is how you fill the warehouse with the wrong cases while the line that retailers care about waits.

questions.text: What is the minimum run you will actually accept?
questions.answer: Below a certain case count the changeover labour and flush losses are worse than the margin on the order. We published that threshold last year and finance signed it. Emergency slots keep arriving under that threshold. I can run them if someone accepts the cost and the lost hours on the hero SKUs. Nobody has written that down. Until they do, I will keep batching.

questions.text: If you had one extra week, what would you still not be able to do?
questions.answer: I still could not treat every SKU as if demand were uniform. The equipment does not care that the company grew forty percent. It cares that two flavours now want the same filler. Extra overtime helps a little. It does not delete a two-hour changeover. I wish planning would stop sending me a single percentage and start sending me a ranked list of SKUs and markets.

stakeholders.name: Rakesh Memon
stakeholders.blurb: Working capital, stock-holding, and cost of short runs
stakeholders.sideNote: Rakesh sees cash, inventory value, and run-cost exceptions. He is not in the weekly demand meeting unless someone invites him.

questions.text: Where is working capital actually tied up right now?
questions.answer: Finished goods value is not low. It is sitting in the wrong mix. We have plenty of slower SKUs at plan, and we are thin on the two lines that retailers are shouting about. Safety stock policy is still written as weeks-of-cover at category level, not SKU and channel. From finance this looks like we funded inventory, just not the inventory that is under threat.

questions.text: Were you consulted on emergency replenishment?
questions.answer: No. I saw a draft of overtime and spot-buy premiums after the conversation had already started with sales. Short runs destroy the cost standard we use to price these products. If we approve them silently, the P&L will show a manufacturing variance and nobody will remember it was a commercial choice. I would rather be in the room when someone decides that a six-week delisting risk is worth breaking the run-length rule.

questions.text: What does stock-holding policy allow you to do in the next six weeks?
questions.answer: Policy still caps cover on low-velocity SKUs, which is sensible, but it also makes it hard to pre-build the fast movers without an exception. Exceptions need a named owner. Right now operations is asking for cash, sales is asking for cases, and the policy sits in a PDF. I can fund a targeted build if someone shows me SKU-level risk. I will not fund a blanket 40 percent uplift that treats every bottle the same.

questions.text: What would a bad problem statement cost you?
questions.answer: If we call this a forecasting failure and pour money into overall volume, we will add stock where we already have it and still miss the accounts that matter. Write-offs and discounts will show up a quarter later. If we call it pure capacity, we will approve capex conversations we cannot execute in six weeks. I need a framing that names mix, cash, and which customers are actually at risk.

evidence.title: Retailer Complaints Summary
evidence.subtitle: Distributor and modern trade feedback — last 21 days
evidence.teaser: Understand which retail partners are escalating, which markets are affected, and whether delisting risk is broad or concentrated.

blocks.text: Customer operations logged 47 availability complaints in the last 21 days. The volume of tickets is not evenly spread. A small set of modern trade banners in UAE and KSA account for most of the severity, including the two written delisting threats. Several hospitality and convenience accounts in Qatar reported no material gaps in the same window.

evidence.title: Production Capacity & Changeover Memo
evidence.subtitle: Factory constraints, utilisation, and run-length rules
evidence.teaser: Review plant-level constraints, changeover hours, and what manufacturing says can realistically move in six weeks.
evidence.sourceLabel: Plant operations memo · Dubai factory · 27 Aug 2026

blocks.text: The Dubai plant runs three beverage lines. Lines 1 and 2 handle the juice SKUs that are currently short. Changeovers between citrus and mango require a full flush. Line 3 (tea and water) is not the constraint this month. The memo restates the minimum economic run length agreed with finance last year.

blocks.caption: Line utilisation and changeover hours — last four weeks

blocks.label: Minimum economic run length
blocks.text: Juice SKUs below 18,000 cases per campaign are treated as uneconomic on Lines 1 and 2. Several emergency requests this month sat between 6,000 and 12,000 cases.

items: Protect current campaigns on Lines 1 and 2 unless a named commercial exception is signed.
Do not break a citrus run for a sub-threshold mango request without costing the lost hours.
Line 3 overtime does not relieve juice shortages.
A ranked SKU list from planning is required before any extra Saturday crew is booked.

submission.prompt: In one paragraph, state the problem your team believes is worth solving. Be specific about what is happening, where, and why a generic 'we need more stock' framing may or may not be enough. This is a judgement, not a score.
